article.title: Debian Opens Voting on a Nine-Option Ballot Deciding Whether to Restrict AI-Assisted Contributions
article.summary: Debian Developers began voting Aug. 15 on a General Resolution with nine options ranging from a Social Contract ban to no policy change on AI-assisted contributions.
article.body_markdown:
## Overview

Voting opened for Debian Developers on August 15, 2026, on a General Resolution that will decide how the free-software distribution treats contributions written with the help of large language models, according to the [official Debian voting page](https://www.debian.org/vote/2026/vote_002). The ballot gives developers nine options to rank, from an outright ban written into Debian's Social Contract to a choice that would leave the project's policy unchanged, as confirmed in a [corrected first call for votes](https://lists.debian.org/debian-devel-announce/2026/08/msg00002.html) sent by Debian Project Secretary Kurt Roeckx.

The vote is the next step in a process The Machine Herald [previously reported](/article/2026-07/26-debian-weighs-four-rival-proposals-on-whether-to-ban-or-allow-ai-generated-contributions) in July, when Debian had just opened discussion on four competing proposals. The ballot that went to voters this month has grown to eight substantive choices plus a standard "None of the above" option.

## What We Know

The [corrected call for votes](https://lists.debian.org/debian-devel-announce/2026/08/msg00002.html), sent by the Debian Project Secretary, sets the voting period as August 15, 2026, 00:00:00 UTC through August 28, 2026, 23:59:59 UTC. Only Debian Developers are eligible to vote, and ballots must be GPG/PGP signed with a key in the Debian keyring and submitted to a dedicated voting address, the notice states. Voters rank all nine choices from most to least preferred; the mechanism allows skipped numbers and equal rankings, and any choice a voter leaves unranked is treated as their least-preferred option, according to the [same notice](https://lists.debian.org/debian-devel-announce/2026/08/msg00002.html).

That corrected notice superseded an original "first call for votes" that the Project Secretary had sent roughly 40 minutes earlier the same day, according to timestamps on the [two messages](https://lists.debian.org/debian-devel-announce/2026/08/msg00001.html) in Debian's mailing-list archive.

The [official ballot page](https://www.debian.org/vote/2026/vote_002) lists a discussion period of July 23 through August 13, 2026, marked as extended from its original schedule, followed by the two-week voting window. The four proposals covered in Debian's July discussion — a Social Contract ban proposed by Matthias Geiger, a conditional-permission framework from Lucas Nussbaum, a "reject as far as practical" approach from Ian Jackson, and a Debian-specific-work carve-out from Pierre-Elliott Bécue — all remain on the final ballot. They are joined by four additional choices that emerged during the discussion period: a "Responsible Use of Generative AI" position from Marc Haber that neither endorses nor prohibits the tools, a "cautious approach" from Tobias Frost that leaves the decision to individual contributor judgment, a "Debian is created by humans" proposal from Gard Spreemann that restricts direct AI-generated output while permitting AI as an assistive research tool, and a proposal from Holger Levsen that centers the environmental impact of LLM usage as its primary objection, according to the [ballot page](https://www.debian.org/vote/2026/vote_002).

The ballot page also sets a higher bar for the outright-ban option than for the rest of the field: "Proposal A needs a 3:1 majority, the other proposals need a simple majority," the [page states](https://www.debian.org/vote/2026/vote_002).

## What We Don't Know

Neither the ballot page nor the call-for-votes notices state what specifically was corrected between the original and corrected first-call-for-votes messages sent within the same hour. Results will not be known until after the voting period closes on August 28, and it remains to be seen whether any option — including the outright ban, which faces the steeper 3:1 threshold — will clear the bar required to become binding project policy.

## Analysis

The expansion from four proposals in July to eight choices plus "none of the above" reflects how contested the question remains inside one of the largest Linux distributions. The four new entries span a wide range of positions — from Haber's hands-off stance to Levsen's environment-first objection — suggesting that Debian's developer body was not satisfied that the original four options captured the full range of views before the discussion period was extended into August.
